text: Chapter five gave you a scoped application to build inside. This chapter gives you something real to build in it: a custom application's own tables, forms, and modules, starting with the design work most teams skip and regret skipping later.

Before any table gets a name, write down the real entities — the actual things this application needs to track, not the screens you imagine building. A Facilities conference-room booking app needs exactly two. A Room: a physical space with a name, a building, and a seating capacity, that simply exists whether or not anyone ever books it. And a Room Booking: a specific request from a specific employee, which has to move through a real lifecycle from submitted to approved or denied to completed.

Ask one question of each entity: does it need to be routed, approved, or tracked through a state machine? Room Booking clearly does — it needs states like Requested, Approved, Denied, and Completed, plus an assignment group for whoever resolves room conflicts. That's exactly the shared behavior extending task provides for free, the same way it does for incident and change request. Room doesn't need any of that — it has no lifecycle, so giving it a state field and an assignment group would only confuse a static reference record. Room Booking extends task; Room stands alone, with no parent at all.

Now plan the relationship from both directions. Room Booking gets a reference field, room, pointing at the Room table — storing a sys_id behind a readable room name, the exact reference-field pattern Course 2 covered. The reverse view belongs on Room's own form: a related list showing every booking that points back at that specific room. Planning both directions now, before any table exists, means neither side of the relationship gets forgotten once the application is already in daily use.

Extend task when an entity needs workflow, routing, or approval; stand alone when it's static, descriptive, lookup-style data. Plan the reference field and the related list on the other side of it before you build either table. Lesson 25 takes this exact design and turns it into real tables, form layouts, list layouts, and the module record that finally makes them reachable from the Application Navigator.
